2.text: This method resembles that of the Pacific Koryak, where the young

3.text: people cover their faces with wooden masks and go from house to house,

4.text: asking in pantomime for various things. The givers have the right either to

5.text: send their children immediately for an equivalent, or to wait till the next

6.text: ceremonial, when their young people may, in their turn, ask for presents.

7.text: On St. Lawrence Island, young boys and girls arrange themselves in

8.text: small processions, which go from house to house, dancing, and asking for

9.text: gifts, mostly of food. This is done some time in winter and has no connection

10.text: with the regular ceremonials, and the practice strongly resembles the customs

11.text: of the Pacific Koryak as described above.

12.text: I must also mention that a similar performance has been in favor among

13.text: the Russians from very remote times. In the first days of Christmastide, at

14.text: dusk, young persons of both sexes go from house to house, singing, dancing,

15.text: and asking for presents. They bedeck themselves in fantastic attire, and wear

16.text: masks. The songs are called “koliada,” and the whole performance is thought

17.text: by ethnographists to be a remnant of a winter ceremonial of Russian Slavs

18.text: in honor of the deity Koliada. This name is associated with the Roman

19.text: calends. Be this as it may, the same practice is found also in northeastern

20.text: Siberia, among the cossacks and Russian creoles; for instance, in the Russian

21.text: villages of the Kolyma, Anadyr, and Kamchatka, and even among the Rus-

22.text: sianized natives in the same localities. It must be assumed, however, that

23.text: the performances of the Koryak and St. Lawrence Eskimo are quite indepen-

24.text: dent, notwithstanding their resemblance to those of the Russians.

25.text: In arctic Chukchee villages the exchange is often arranged in the fol-

26.text: lowing manner. On the first day of the ceremonial, at the height of the

27.text: drumming and singing, every guest who desires something belonging to the

28.text: master must strike his left palm with his right fist, and exclaim, “I see such-

29.text: and-such a thing!” The master must immediately give it away; and after the

30.text: ceremonial is finished, he may ask for an equivalent. Should the thing asked

31.text: for be something of exceeding great value, the master may refuse the demand,

32.text: lifting his right thumb to his throat, and exclaiming, “I would (rather) cut

33.text: my throat!” This, however, is considered a great offence, and may even lead

35.text: Many families arrange the exchange between relatives only, and espe-

36.text: cially between those joined by the bond of compound marriage, literally “wife-

37.text: companions” (ñew-tuˊmg̣ɪt). A man sends his wife to another man with whom

38.text: he is connected by such a bond to ask for certain wares, and after a while

39.text: the other man sends his wife to ask for an equivalent.

40.text: The Trading-Dance. — This brings us to another variety of the cere-

41.text: monial exchange, which may be called “trading-dance.” It is performed during

42.text: the second day of the ceremonial by couples, a man and a woman each, who
